lead: Two hymns of praise stand side by side today. Ephesians opens with a great blessing of God for his plan, chosen “before the foundation of the world” and fulfilled in Christ. Luke gives us the Magnificat, Mary’s song for what God has done for her and for his people. One hymn looks at God’s plan from eternity; the other sees it come true in a humble young woman of Nazareth.

r.h: Blessed be the God and Father
set: In Greek, verses 3–14 form one single long sentence, a hymn that seems to run out of breath in praise. It takes the form of the Jewish berakah, a prayer that begins “Blessed be God” and then lists his works. Paul blesses the Father for what he has done in Christ, and the passage moves from eternity (v. 4) to the fullness of time (v. 10).
str: v. 3: the blessing of the Father for every spiritual blessing in Christ.
vv. 4–6: chosen and destined to be his adopted children.
vv. 7–8: redemption through his blood and forgiveness.
vv. 9–10: the mystery of his will: to gather up all things in Christ.
vv. 11–12: our inheritance, so that we may live for the praise of his glory.
kw: God blesses us with gifts; we bless God with praise. The same word goes down and comes back up.
Literally “to bring under one head”. St Irenaeus built his teaching of “recapitulation” on this word: Christ takes up the whole story of humanity and of creation and heals it in himself.
Not a riddle but God’s hidden plan, now revealed. The Syriac tradition speaks of raza, the mystery made present in the liturgy.
vv: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places,
just as he chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world to be holy and blameless before him in love.
Before anything existed, God thought of us in his Son. The aim of the choice is holiness, and its atmosphere is love.
as a plan for the fullness of time, to gather up all things in him, things in heaven and things on earth.
The whole universe has one centre and one goal: Christ.
ch: The Catechism opens its teaching on the liturgy with this hymn: in the liturgy the Father is blessed as the source of every blessing (CCC 1077–1078). It also calls God’s plan, revealed in Ephesians 1, a “plan of loving kindness” conceived before the creation of the world (CCC 257).

set: Mary has gone in haste to visit Elizabeth, and Elizabeth has called her “blessed” (1:42–45). Mary answers not by speaking about herself but by praising God. Her song is woven from Old Testament texts, above all the song of Hannah (1 Samuel 2:1–10), another woman whose child was God’s gift.
str: vv. 46–50: what God has done for Mary.
vv. 51–53: what God does in the world: the proud scattered, the lowly lifted up.
vv. 54–55: what God has done for Israel, faithful to his promise to Abraham.
kw: To make great, to declare great. Mary cannot make God greater, but she makes his greatness known.
Low estate, humble condition. It is not first a virtue Mary claims but the smallness God chose to look upon.
In the Greek Old Testament it often renders the Hebrew ḥesed, God’s faithful covenant love. The word appears at the centre (v. 50) and the end (v. 54) of the song.
vv: for he has looked with favor on the lowliness of his servant. Surely, from now on all generations will call me blessed;
A prophecy fulfilled every time the Church honours Mary. Her blessedness comes from God’s look, not from her own greatness.
He has brought down the powerful from their thrones, and lifted up the lowly;
The verbs are in the past tense, as if God’s reversal were already done. In Christ it has begun.
according to the promise he made to our ancestors, to Abraham and to his descendants forever.
The song ends with Abraham. What God is doing in Mary is the fulfilment of a very old promise.
ch: The Catechism calls the Magnificat “the song both of the Mother of God and of the Church” (CCC 2619). St Ambrose, commenting on this Gospel, wishes that the soul of Mary be in each of us to magnify the Lord, and her spirit in each of us to rejoice in God (in substance).

qa: Did Mary really compose such a hymn?

Mary was a young Jewish woman whose prayer was formed by the psalms and the songs of Scripture. The Magnificat is built from those texts, as a devout person of her time could pray. A few old Latin manuscripts attribute the song to Elizabeth, but almost all manuscripts and the whole tradition of the Church give it to Mary.
study: Ephesians says God chose me “before the foundation of the world”. How would my day change if I truly believed this?
Mary praises God for looking on her lowliness. Where in my life do I need to let God look on my smallness rather than hide it?
